issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'being followed or tracked' suggests an interpersonal/persecutory trauma context that is not supported by the other selected items and is hard to reconcile with the trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by interpersonal assault-style vigilance to sounds and sudden movements, which does not fit well with the stated trauma of toxic chemical exposure unless there is additional unreported violent context.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies mistrust of others in a deceptive or persecutory sense; paired with 'being followed' it shifts the formulation toward interpersonal threat rather than contamination/exposure-related PTSD.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'Avoid authority figures' is difficult to connect to the rest of the profile and to toxic chemical exposure specifically; no other items indicate authority-linked fear, blame, or trauma reminders involving uniforms/institutions.

vignette: María, a 57-year-old Latina detective from Chicago, has been dealing with the aftermath of her exposure to toxic chemicals at a crime scene three months ago. The incident occurred during what should have been another routine investigation, but the unexpected release of dangerous substances turned it into a life-altering experience. On that fateful day, María was working alone in an abandoned warehouse investigating evidence from a series of chemical-related crimes. As she approached one of the storage containers, there was an eerie silence broken only by her own footsteps echoing through the empty space. Suddenly, a cloud of noxious gas enveloped her, and she found herself struggling to breathe as the air became thick with the acrid smell of chemicals. The immediate physical distress triggered María's fight-or-flight response. She frantically searched for a way out, but each breath was more labored than the last. Panic set in as she realized that her body was not responding the way it should have; she felt weak and disoriented, struggling to make sense of what was happening. In her mind, the incident didn't just end there-it remained fragmented, with disconnected pieces that wouldn't fit together coherently. Since then, María has been plagued by triggers that evoke a visceral response reminiscent of that moment. The smell of sweat or body odor-a common occurrence in her line of work-immediately sends her into a state of high alert, as if she is reliving the toxic exposure. Even the faintest trace of antiseptic scent from hospitals can jolt her back to the overwhelming fear and breathlessness. Her hypervigilance has become a constant presence in her life. María finds herself scanning her surroundings constantly for any signs of danger, always on edge and prepared to react at a moment's notice. Her body feels perpetually tense, as if she is bracing for another attack. The experience has left her with a deep sense of distrust towards authority figures and institutions that should have protected her but did not. To cope with the overwhelming anxiety, María has developed several maladaptive strategies. When confronted with triggers like the smell of sweat or antiseptic, she often covers her face with her hands to block out the sensations and push away any intrusive memories before they can fully resurface. She also employs redirection techniques, shifting her focus to other thoughts when faced with overwhelming emotions or environmental cues. This constant state of vigilance has taken a toll on María's work as well. Her aversion to being around authority figures or people in uniforms has made it difficult for her to collaborate effectively with colleagues and superiors. She avoids situations where she might be required to interact closely with uniformed officers, leading to strained relationships at the precinct and decreased job satisfaction. Over time, these avoidance behaviors have compounded into significant consequences. Her ability to perform investigative work has been compromised as she frequently pushes away critical memories before they can provide valuable insights into her cases. She is certain that this institutional failure means no one will ever be able to protect her adequately again, and this belief only exacerbates her sense of vulnerability. The memory of the toxic exposure feels like it is happening all over again, rather than something in the past. The fragmented nature of these memories leaves María with a profound feeling of disconnection from herself and her environment. She has come to believe that she will never be able to feel normal emotions again; the experience seems to have permanently altered her emotional landscape. What finally brought María to seek help was a recent incident at work where she nearly relived the toxic exposure while processing evidence in an air-conditioned room filled with faint chemical odors. The fear and breathlessness were overwhelming, and she realized that her coping mechanisms were no longer sufficient. She is most afraid of losing control completely and becoming unable to function both professionally and personally. María hopes for a return to some semblance of normalcy-emotional stability and the ability to trust again without constant hypervigilance. While seeking help, she remains wary but also hopeful that therapy will provide her with tools to manage her symptoms effectively and regain control over her life.
